cards.title: UKRI Future Leaders Fellowships
cards.post: UKRI Future Leaders Fellowships are long fellowships for early-career researchers, with a 4+3 year structure, and need internal support from the host institution. Next deadline: 16 February 2027.
cards.why_you: Well matched to your postdoctoral fellowship search, provided Imperial runs its internal selection in time.

cards.title: HFSP Postdoctoral Fellowships
cards.post: HFSP Postdoctoral Fellowships fund three-year fellowships for researchers moving to a new field and a new country, within three years of their PhD. The Letter of Intent initiation deadline is 4 May 2027, with submission by 11 May 2027. Next deadline: 4 May 2027.
cards.why_you: Your PhD window fits the three-year limit, and the programme's push for high-risk interdisciplinary work suits your computational and neurodynamics interests.

cards.why_you: Wellcome's mental health calls could suit your psychedelic and depression work, though no current call with a deadline is visible yet.

cards.title: Rosetrees Trust – research funding
cards.post: Rosetrees Trust is a UK private charity funding early-career and project medical research, applied for through the host institution. The page text gives no specific call or deadline.
cards.why_you: As a UK early-career researcher, Rosetrees could fund neurology-adjacent work, though its listed projects focus mainly on clinical and disease areas.

cards.title: UKRI Translation: MRC Impact Acceleration Awards
cards.post: UKRI MRC Impact Acceleration Awards fund a single high-risk development step to de-risk a new medicine, device, diagnostic or other medical product. Open to staff at MRC-eligible research organisations. Deadline not stated in the page text.
cards.why_you: Only loosely relevant: aimed at product translation rather than your basic PET and psychedelic research, though a clinical pharmacology step could fit.

cards.title: ICPR – Interdisciplinary Conference on Psychedelic Research
cards.post: ICPR 2028, the Interdisciplinary Conference on Psychedelic Research, takes place in Haarlem, Netherlands, from 7 to 10 June 2028. It is held every two years and is Europe's main psychedelic research meeting.
cards.why_you: This is the main European meeting for psychedelic research, directly relevant to your work on DMT, psilocybin and ketamine.

cards.why_you: As a UK-based researcher, the BNA meeting offers networking and early-career visibility for your work on psychedelics and brain imaging.

cards.title: CNS* – Computational Neuroscience Meeting

cards.why_you: Neural mass models and criticality match your neurodynamics interests, and the meeting is a good venue to present EEG complexity work.

cards.title: Neural and Experiential Dynamics of High-Ventilation Breathwork Mirror Psychedelic States
cards.post: Aim: Whether the neural dynamics evoked by high-ventilation breathwork resemble those of classical psychedelic states, and whether they track subjective experience depth. Methods: 64-channel EEG in 25 experienced breathwork practitioners, with resting-state recordings interleaved through a naturalistic high-ventilation breathwork session; experience depth and content also recorded. Results: Breathwork produced broadband cortical desynchronisation, higher signal complexity, reduced alpha power and flattened cortical hierarchy, with these effects correlating with subjective depth at minute resolution. The effects were not explained by music listening or active interoception. Conclusion: The authors argue these are shared neural features of psychedelic-like states regardless of induction method, so breathwork may access psychedelic-like cortical states without drugs.
cards.why_you: Directly relevant to your EEG complexity and criticality work, and to brain–body coupling via breath, as a non-pharmacological route to psychedelic-like cortical dynamics.

cards.title: Changes in self-related cognitive processes and depressive symptom severity following a single, moderate dose of psilocybin in depressed patients.
cards.venue: Philosophical transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B, Biological sciences
cards.post: Aim: Whether a single moderate psilocybin dose changes self-concept and self-referential neural processing alongside depressive symptoms in major depressive disorder. Methods: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; N = 37 with major depressive disorder given 0.215 mg/kg psilocybin or placebo with psychological support; depression scales, self-concept scale and fMRI self-referential task. Results: Psilocybin reduced depressive symptoms and increased positive self-concept two weeks after dosing relative to placebo, with self-concept change correlated with lower depression scores. Caudate activation was modulated during externally oriented attention after psilocybin, versus self-referential processing after placebo. Conclusion: The authors conclude self-concept and self-referential processing change concurrently with symptom reduction, and call for replication and refined self-focused therapy protocols.
cards.why_you: Links psilocybin's clinical effects to self-processing and fMRI, close to your psilocybin-for-depression interests and the clinical pharmacology strand.
cards.why_picked: psilocybin · depressive · by Franz Vollenweider, Katrin Preller · close to your paper “Serotonergic psychedelics for depression: A…” · Claude 4/5

cards.title: The 5-HT2A receptor inverse agonist/antagonist volinanserin modulates motor outcomes and regulates lateral septum-prefrontal and lateral septum-hippocampal functional connectivity.
cards.post: Aim: How the 5-HT2A inverse agonist volinanserin affects behaviour and circuit-level brain activity and connectivity in mice, relevant to schizophrenia. Methods: Behavioural battery in mice covering motor, anxiety-like, compulsive-like, reward and learning domains, with brain activity and functional connectivity measured for drug versus vehicle. Results: Volinanserin selectively reduced locomotor activity, leaving anxiety, compulsive-like behaviour, reward and learning unaffected. It raised activity in the lateral septum, dorsal raphe and nucleus accumbens, lowered prefrontal activity, and reduced lateral septum connectivity with prefrontal cortex, hippocampus and amygdala. Conclusion: The authors conclude the lateral septum is a key locus for volinanserin's putative antipsychotic effects, supporting its role in 5-HT2A-targeting drug action.
cards.why_you: Relevant to 5-HT2A pharmacology and circuit-level connectivity, though it is a mouse study outside your human imaging work.

cards.title: Exploring subacute effects of a DMT and harmine meditation retreat on the brain's control energy landscape
cards.post: Aim: Whether a DMT and harmine meditation retreat changes the brain's control energy landscape in the subacute afterglow window. Methods: Exploratory analysis of rs-fMRI from a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (N = 39) before and after a three-day retreat, with control energy computed on a group structural connectome under two timescale approaches. Results: No global shift in control energy between transitions, though mean control energy rose in both groups under the long-timescale approach. The central executive network showed a post-retreat increase in the verum group surviving FDR correction, and the visual network decreased under the short-timescale approach. Conclusion: The authors conclude effects are network- and timescale-specific rather than global, but small, heterogeneous and needing confirmation in larger samples.
cards.why_you: Applies network control theory to psychedelic afterglow effects, connecting to your neurodynamics and whole-brain modelling interests.

cards.title: Quantitative Analysis of Lysergic Acid Diethylamide: A Ring Study Among Five Swiss Drug Checking Services.
cards.post: Aim: Whether LSD quantification across Swiss drug checking laboratories is accurate and reproducible. Methods: Interlaboratory ring trial across five Swiss drug checking services using HPLC-DAD, GC-MS and HPLC-MS/MS on two LSD-infused blotters and one methanolic solution, with results corrected by qNMR-determined purity. Results: Relative standard deviations were 8%–16.5% and mean accuracy −5.3% to −13.0%, with more variability for the liquid sample and the largest deviations from mass spectrometry methods. Conclusion: The authors conclude current LSD quantification is reliable in drug checking settings and provide a basis for future proficiency testing, noting stability and production factors as possible sources of discrepancy.
cards.why_you: Peripheral to your PET and neuroimaging work, though it bears on dose accuracy in psychedelic research and harm reduction.

cards.title: From Rapid Synaptic Events to Lasting Antidepressant States: Convergent and Divergent Mechanisms of Ketamine and Psychedelics.
cards.venue: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
cards.post: Aim: What mechanisms underlie the rapid and lasting antidepressant effects of ketamine and classical psychedelics, centred on synaptic and circuit plasticity. Methods: Narrative review, based on a 2026 Society for Neuroscience minisymposium, covering hippocampal, prefrontal and accumbal mechanisms for ketamine and comparing these with psilocybin. Results: Review of BDNF/TrkB, mGluR5, ERK-DUSP6 and GPCR-dependent plasticity mechanisms across regions and cell types for ketamine, with psilocybin's 5-HT2A-mediated effects compared. Conclusion: The authors argue antidepressant efficacy arises from coordinated, temporally staged plasticity across molecules, synapses, cells and circuits rather than a single pathway.
cards.why_you: Closely matches your work on ketamine and psychedelics as neuroplastogens and the plasticity markers you study in humans.

cards.title: Mechanisms of Psychedelic Metaplasticity: Intracellular Receptor Pharmacology, Epigenomic Priming and Candidate Substrates of Persistence-A Narrative Review.
cards.post: Aim: What candidate substrates could sustain the persistent effects of a single psychedelic dose across the days-to-weeks consolidation window. Methods: Narrative review of intracellular 5-HT2A pools, neurotrophin convergence and cortical H3K27ac epigenomic data, with evidence graded as established, indirect or hypothetical and six falsifiable criteria proposed. Results: Cited data show persistent bidirectional H3K27ac changes at seven days in mouse frontal cortex after one compound, interpreted as a displaced regulatory set-point rather than a retained mark. Conclusion: The authors conclude the evidence is narrow and that claims of persistence over weeks concern behaviour rather than chromatin state, offering falsifiable tests.
cards.why_you: Engages the persistence question central to your plasticity and metaplasticity interests, with a useful critique of the epigenomic evidence.

cards.title: First-in-class -PET radiotracers for GPR39: A platform for noninvasive target engagement imaging in vivo
cards.post: Aim: Whether the fluorine-18 PET radiotracer [18F]GPR39 2.1 can specifically image the zinc-sensing receptor GPR39 in vivo. Methods: Preclinical study in cell uptake assays, rats with pharmacological blockade, GPR39 knockout mice, 5xFAD transgenic mice, PET imaging, biodistribution and autoradiography. Results: Brain uptake fell by up to about 90% under blockade in rats, by 76% by PET and 90% by biodistribution in knockout mice, and was reduced in 5xFAD mice, with good stability and brain penetration. Conclusion: The authors conclude [18F]GPR39 2.1 is a stable, brain-penetrant and highly specific tracer for noninvasive GPR39 imaging, supporting its use as an imaging and therapeutic target.
cards.why_you: A new PET tracer with blockade and knockout validation, relevant to your PET radiotracer and target engagement methods.

cards.title: A shared slowing axis and phenotype-specific rhythms link clinical EEG to FDG-PET dementia phenotypes
cards.post: Aim: Whether data-driven factors from clinical EEG differ across FDG-PET-defined neurodegenerative dementia phenotypes. Methods: 455 patients with EEG and FDG-PET within one year; six EEG factors from nonnegative tensor decomposition compared across 14 StateViewer diagnostic classes, adjusted for a slowing index and related to regional metabolism and cognition (n = 98). Results: Four oscillatory factors varied across phenotypes, most strongly in dementia with Lewy bodies, dysexecutive Alzheimer disease and posterior cortical atrophy. Slowing explained much of the alpha and beta effects, while posterior theta-slow alpha stayed phenotype-specific after adjustment. Conclusion: The authors conclude decomposed clinical EEG separates oscillatory activity from artefact in ways tracking metabolic phenotype, supporting scalable EEG-based dementia phenotyping, though frontotemporal phenotypes were poorly discriminated.
cards.why_you: Connects EEG spectral decomposition to PET metabolic phenotypes, bridging your EEG and PET interests.

cards.title: A novel theta-frequency tACS approach for major depressive disorder: Initial findings from an open-label pilot study.
cards.post: Aim: Whether individualised theta-frequency tACS over the prefrontal cortex is feasible and tolerable in moderate-to-severe major depressive disorder, and what clinical and EEG changes accompany it. Methods: Open-label pilot of 11 adults with MDD receiving 20 sessions of bilateral prefrontal theta tACS (1.5 mA peak-to-peak, 20 min) during working memory tasks, with frequency individualised from task EEG; 10 completed treatment. Results: MADRS scores fell significantly from baseline to midpoint, endpoint and follow-up. Response rates were 80% and remission 60% at endpoint, rising to 80% and 70% at follow-up. Greater ITF power increases tracked larger MADRS reductions, though group-level power changes were not significant. Conclusion: The authors conclude that the approach is feasible and provides preliminary observations to inform sham-controlled trials, cautioning that the open-label design and small sample limit interpretation and allow placebo effects.
cards.why_you: Relevant to your interest in theta oscillations and neurodynamic markers, and to TMS-EEG and EEG-based biomarkers in depression.

cards.title: Multishell diffusion MRI models have limited sensitivity to ketamine-induced microstructural changes in the mouse brain
cards.post: Aim: Whether multishell diffusion MRI models can detect ketamine-induced dendritic and synaptic microstructural changes in mouse brain in vivo. Methods: In vivo multishell dMRI with diffusion tensor, NODDI and diffusion kurtosis models in wild-type and SAPAP3 knockout mice after ketamine, with histology for synapse markers and Monte Carlo simulations of dendritic diffusion. Results: Histology confirmed ketamine-induced increases in cortical synapse markers, but dMRI metrics did not change. Simulations showed sensitivity to small morphological changes only in noiseless conditions, whereas the acquisitions detected baseline differences between sexes and genotypes. Conclusion: The authors conclude that the dMRI acquisition and modelling approaches used lack sensitivity to the subtle dendritic changes induced by ketamine.
cards.why_you: Directly relevant to your ketamine neuroplastogen work and to finding in vivo biomarkers of plasticity alongside PET synaptic density imaging.

cards.title: Testing an accelerated transcranial magnetic stimulation protocol for methamphetamine use disorder — study protocol
cards.post: Aim: Whether an accelerated iTBS protocol over the left DLPFC is safe, feasible and shows preliminary efficacy in methamphetamine use disorder. Methods: Single-site, randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled pilot planned for 20 adults with moderate-to-severe MUD, receiving up to 40 iTBS or sham sessions over five inpatient days, then weekly follow-up for 12 weeks. Results: Not reported; this is a study protocol describing primary outcomes of safety, tolerability and feasibility, with use, craving and MRI measures as secondary and exploratory outcomes. Conclusion: The authors state that if the pilot proves safe, feasible and shows preliminary efficacy, it would justify larger studies and could offer a scalable short-stay TMS model.
cards.why_you: Links to your interest in TMS and psychiatric neuromodulation, and the MRI resting-state network outcomes fit your neurodynamics interests.

cards.title: Testing the impact of cannabinoid stimulation on fatty acid amide hydrolase binding in the human brain: pilot [11C]CURB PET study
cards.post: Aim: Whether repeated administration of the cannabinoid agonist nabilone changes brain FAAH availability measured with [11C]CURB PET. Methods: Exploratory Phase IV pilot with ten healthy adults, each scanned at baseline and after a 7-day nabilone regimen titrated to 2 mg/day; FAAH quantified with a two-tissue irreversible model and analysed with repeated-measures ANCOVA including genotype. Results: Nabilone increased marijuana-like effects (p = 0.004) and reduced energy (p = 0.02) and clear-headedness (p = 0.01). No detectable mean change in FAAH across brain regions was observed (p = 0.357). Conclusion: The authors conclude that no detectable change in brain FAAH followed seven days of nabilone, a preliminary finding needing confirmation in larger controlled studies.
cards.why_you: A PET study with a novel tracer and a repeated-scan pharmacological design that closely matches your PET kinetic modelling and clinical pharmacology work.

cards.title: 2-AG as a potential biomarker for predicting response to short-term fluoxetine treatment in a mouse model of depression.
cards.post: Aim: Whether endocannabinoid or neurotransmitter levels in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex predict early behavioural response to fluoxetine in a mouse depression model. Methods: Male mice exposed to five weeks of chronic unpredictable mild stress, with fluoxetine during the final week; LC-MS/MS metabolomics of hippocampal and prefrontal cortex samples. Results: Improved behaviour after short-term fluoxetine was accompanied by increased hippocampal 2-AG, and reduced prefrontal GABA and glutamate levels. Conclusion: The authors suggest that increased 2-AG may predict early response to fluoxetine, pointing to it as a candidate biomarker.
cards.why_you: Connects the endocannabinoid system with antidepressant response, relevant to your interest in biomarkers and the broader psychedelic and plasticity questions around serotonergic drugs.

cards.title: Stress-induced dorsal striatal dopamine release is associated with changes in functional connectivity to the prefrontal cortex in nicotine-dependent individuals-a preliminary report.
cards.post: Aim: Whether stress-induced dopamine release in the striatum relates to changes in striatal-prefrontal functional connectivity in nicotine-dependent individuals. Methods: Within-subject multimodal study in eight smokers using endotoxin (LPS) or placebo, with [11C]raclopride PET before and after methylphenidate and seed-based resting-state fMRI. Results: LPS raised cortisol and striatal dopamine release relative to placebo (p < 0.05); cortisol increases correlated with dorsal striatal release (r = 0.708, p = 0.04). Connectivity between striatum and vmPFC and dlPFC increased (p < 0.001, FDR-corrected), with a non-linear stress relationship. Conclusion: The authors suggest stress-related frontal-striatal connectivity changes reflect adaptation, while excessive stress may disrupt circuits, though the small pilot needs replication.
cards.why_you: Combines PET dopamine measures with resting-state connectivity, closely matching your PET methods and your interest in neurodynamics and addiction.
cards.why_picked: dopamine · nicotine-dependent · fMRI · close to your paper “Detecting neuroplastic effects induced by ketamine in…”

cards.title: Nogo-related frontal theta-band activity after magnetic seizure therapy in treatment-resistant depression: an exploratory task-based EEG study.
cards.post: Aim: Whether magnetic seizure therapy in treatment-resistant depression is associated with changes in task-based EEG markers of conflict monitoring and response inhibition. Methods: Open-label single-arm trial in 19 patients with TRD (10 minors), receiving 6-12 MST sessions at F3/F4, with clinical scales and a 64-channel Go/Nogo EEG task before and after treatment. Results: Depression scores fell substantially (HAMD 40.5 to 22.5; MADRS 35.7 to 20.7), with response rates of 42.1-57.9%. Nogo-related frontal theta was lower at an uncorrected threshold but did not survive FDR correction; ERP and microstate changes were not significant. Conclusion: The authors conclude the findings are preliminary, given the absence of a control group, incomplete behavioural data and the lack of corrected EEG effects.

sections: Aim
Whether magnetic seizure therapy in treatment-resistant depression is associated with changes in task-based EEG markers of conflict monitoring and response inhibition.
Methods
Open-label single-arm trial in 19 patients with TRD (10 minors), receiving 6-12 MST sessions at F3/F4, with clinical scales and a 64-channel Go/Nogo EEG task before and after treatment.
Results

Depression scores fell substantially (HAMD 40.5 to 22.5; MADRS 35.7 to 20.7), with response rates of 42.1-57.9%. Nogo-related frontal theta was lower at an uncorrected threshold but did not survive FDR correction; ERP and microstate changes were not significant.
Conclusion
The authors conclude the findings are preliminary, given the absence of a control group, incomplete behavioural data and the lack of corrected EEG effects.

cards.title: Virtual reality as a neural state-modulating technology: EEG complexity during VR gameplay versus VR gameplay viewing
cards.post: Aim: Whether EEG signal complexity differs between actively playing immersive virtual reality and passively watching a recording of the same gameplay. Methods: Thirty-six adults randomised to play an immersive VR game or view a first-person gameplay video in the headset, with four EEG complexity measures and flow and ego dissolution questionnaires. Results: VR gameplay was associated with lower EEG complexity across four broadband measures, with large effects at frontal and parietal midline sites (all corrected p < .001). Flow was higher (d = 1.17) and exploratory ego dissolution higher (d = 1.11). Within-condition correlations did not survive correction. Conclusion: The authors conclude that VR can serve as an experimental route to studying how designed experiences shape conscious state, with neural and experiential effects assessed together.
cards.why_you: Applies Lempel-Ziv and entropy EEG complexity to altered states, closely matching your neurodynamics and criticality interests.

cards.title: FDTest: Fluctuation-dissipation theorem as a test for memory effects in brain dynamics.
cards.post: Aim: Whether a generalised fluctuation-dissipation theorem can detect local memory effects in whole-brain dynamics and distinguish wakefulness from deep sleep. Methods: Introduces the FDTest, measuring violations of a generalised fluctuation-dissipation theorem in whole-brain models fitted to human neuroimaging, then individualised models during wakefulness and deep sleep. Results: Memory effects reflected underlying connectivity and were consistently stronger during wakefulness than deep sleep, indicating richer inter-regional dependencies and more integrated dynamics. Conclusion: The authors conclude that local memory is a dynamical marker of brain state and that the FDTest is a principled tool for probing hidden structure in neural dynamics.
cards.why_you: Directly relevant to your whole-brain modelling and neurodynamics work, offering a new way to probe memory in model-based brain dynamics.

cards.title: Aperiodic Exponent as an EEG Marker of Interoceptive Attention during Gastric Fullness
cards.post: Aim: Whether the EEG aperiodic exponent tracks self-perceived gastric fullness and interoceptive attention to the stomach. Methods: EEG recorded in humans while they drank water until fullness, with simultaneous gastric and cardiac measures to index vagal drive and gastric oscillation frequency. Results: Across individuals, the broadband EEG aperiodic exponent flattened after drinking to fullness. Peripheral measures showed increased vagal drive, and changes in cortical aperiodic patterns were associated with changes in gastric oscillation frequency. Conclusion: The authors suggest the EEG aperiodic exponent may be a useful noninvasive biomarker of gastric interoceptive attention.
cards.why_you: Links brain-body coupling and interoception with EEG aperiodic activity, both central to your wider interests in gut-brain signalling and neurodynamics.

cards.title: Neurophysiological correlates of interoceptive compassion training for depression
cards.post: Aim: Whether a four-week interoceptive compassion programme, HST-IIP, changes depression, heartbeat-evoked potentials and Delta activity in people with depression. Methods: Pilot randomised controlled trial of 23 adults with depression, HST-IIP versus waitlist control, with EEG and clinical assessments before and after a four-week intervention. Results: HST-IIP produced greater depression score improvement than control (Hedges' g = -1.422, p = 0.028) and increased interoceptive awareness. Attenuated right frontal heartbeat-evoked potentials and reduced Delta power during compassion meditation were associated with clinical improvement. Conclusion: The authors describe the work as exploratory preliminary evidence; the programme may influence neurophysiological processes relevant to depression, warranting further research.
cards.why_you: Links interoception and heartbeat-evoked potentials, relevant to your brain–body coupling interests and EEG-based markers in depression.

cards.title: EXPRESS: Blood-free full quantification of dynamic TSPO PET imaging with [11C]PBR28.
cards.venue: Journal of cerebral blood flow and metabolism : official journal of the International Society of Cerebral Blood Flow and Metabolism
cards.post: Aim: Whether a deep-learning arterial input function estimate can replace blood sampling for quantitative dynamic TSPO PET with [11C]PBR28. Methods: ASTRA framework developed on 90 participants with arterial data, transfer-learned and tested on 52 at a second centre, applied to a clinical cohort of 32 without arterial data and a blocking cohort of 5. Results: ASTRA-derived VT agreed with arterial measurements (CCC 0.658-0.805). It reproduced SUVR-based group differences using DVR (p<0.001) except in the pituitary gland, and gave receptor occupancy of 0.92 versus 0.94 arterially. Conclusion: The authors conclude multi-site, non-invasive quantitative TSPO PET is feasible, though higher uncertainty accompanies larger error.
cards.why_you: Directly relevant to your PET kinetic modelling work, offering a route to quantification without arterial sampling.

cards.title: Quality of Life and the Case for Consent-Based Psilocybin Access – Questions on the Regulatory Framework and Cost
cards.post: Aim: Whether competent adults should access psilocybin on consent alone, and how regulatory frameworks shape its cost. Methods: Argument-based policy article reviewing legal routes, costs across jurisdictions, safety evidence, scheduling history and a Canadian case. Results: Authorised clinical routes cost far more than non-medical routes, with COMP360 projected near esketamine pricing. Removing diagnosis requirements without subsidy risks replacing regulatory barriers with wealth-based ones. Conclusion: The author argues for consent-based access paired with public subsidy to avoid cost-based exclusion.
cards.why_you: Relevant to your psychedelic clinical work and the access and cost questions raised by upcoming psilocybin approvals.

cards.title: Domain-level symptom improvement after ketamine and TMS-based stimulation in treatment-resistant depression: a post hoc pooled analysis.
cards.post: Aim: Whether ketamine and TMS produce different short-term improvements across depression, anxiety, insomnia and somatic symptom domains. Methods: Post hoc pooled analysis of 159 active-treatment participants from three trials, ketamine infusion (n=89) or two-week TMS (n=70), with domain-level models adjusted for baseline scores, age and sex. Results: Improvement differed across domains within both modalities. Depression improved most (1.48 SD after ketamine, 1.71 after TMS). Between-modality contrasts did not survive adjustment, except the somatic contrast after adjusting for treatment-resistance categories. Conclusion: The authors caution that cross-modality comparisons are exploratory and do not establish equivalence or guide treatment choice.
cards.why_you: Connects ketamine and TMS symptom profiles, relevant to your ketamine plasticity and TMS-EEG interests.

cards.title: Cortical depth EEG-fMRI at 7T: Experimental setup and analysis pipeline to elucidate generating mechanisms of alpha oscillations.
cards.post: Aim: To develop a non-invasive 7T EEG-fMRI framework for studying the generating mechanisms of alpha oscillations across cortical depth. Methods: Simultaneous 7T laminar fMRI and EEG in 10 participants during an eyes-closed/eyes-open paradigm, with a deveining procedure to reduce pial-vein BOLD contamination. Results: In 9 of 10 participants, EEG alpha power correlated negatively with visual cortex BOLD. After deveining, correlations were weaker in middle depths than superficial and deep layers, and this depth dependence disappeared with a boxcar regressor. Conclusion: The authors state the depth profiles are consistent with top-down feedback activity, but causality cannot be definitively demonstrated from these data.
cards.why_you: Directly relevant to your EEG and neurodynamics interests, offering a laminar fMRI approach to oscillation origins.

cards.title: R5 head model for TMS navigation: trained model files (nnU-Net segmenter and MNI warp network)
cards.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
cards.post: Trained model files for TMS navigation head modelling: five nnU-Net segmentation folds and a warp network producing a SimNIBS-format m2m folder in about 35 s on a GPU. Trained on 548 heads, with mean distance to charm of 1.3-1.8 mm at TMS targets. Released under GPL-3.0.
cards.why_you: Could streamline individual head models for your TMS-EEG work without lengthy segmentation.

cards.title: Probabilistic mapping of brain connections without random sampling
cards.post: MPAT, an open-source tool that maps brain connections by modelling tractography as an absorbing Markov chain, giving the expected result of infinitely many streamlines without random sampling. It is reported as more reliable across test–retest scans and usable on clinical-grade data and neonates.
cards.why_you: Offers a deterministic alternative to streamline tractography if you add structural connectivity to whole-brain models.

Poisoned hunting weapons, megafauna, and plant use at a 125,000-year-old Arabian paleolakeshore.
cards.post: Aim: Whether a 125,000-year-old Arabian paleolakeshore site shows hominin tool production, plant processing and poisoned hunting weapons. Methods: Archaeological analysis of Levallois assemblages, refits, megafaunal associations, residues, use-wear and biomarkers at the 'Uruq Aljelibah site, Saudi Arabia. Results: Points show impact damage and Acokanthera schimperi poison residues, indicating hafted weapon tips. Plant processing and megafaunal remains including hippopotamus, buffalo and camel were identified. Conclusion: The authors infer in situ tool production, poisoned composite hunting systems and hominin use of freshwater and grassland ecosystems.
cards.why_you: Outside your fields, but a neuroscientist may find the cognitive complexity implied by poisoned composite weapons interesting.

cards.title: A Neandertal-derived genetic variant reduces occipital brain volume in present-day humans
cards.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
cards.post: Aim: Whether a Neandertal-derived genetic variant influences occipital brain volume and schizophrenia risk in present-day humans. Methods: Genetic association analysis linking a Neandertal-inherited variant near DAAM1 to occipital lobe volume, gene expression, schizophrenia risk and cognitive measures. Results: Carriers had occipital volumes about 0.85 cm³ smaller per gene copy. Homozygous carriers showed almost 10% lower schizophrenia risk, with little or no association with cognition or schooling. Conclusion: The authors conclude the variant alters brain anatomy and lowers schizophrenia risk with little association with general cognitive ability.
cards.why_you: A neuroscientist may find the link between an archaic variant, occipital anatomy and schizophrenia risk of interest.

cards.title: Human land use drives microplastic abundance in terrestrial wildlife.
authors: Marcia de Almeida Monteiro Melo Ferraz
cards.post: Aim: To determine how human land use and the animals' proximity to development shape microplastic burdens in terrestrial wildlife. Methods: In vivo microplastic measurements in blood and tissue of free-ranging lowland tapirs and giant anteaters across Brazil, paired with high-resolution GPS tracking and human footprint exposure data. Results: Microplastic burdens increased with human footprint exposure and proximity to development and waste management infrastructure. Microplastics were also detected in individuals in seemingly pristine habitats far from development. Conclusion: Direct exposure to modified landscapes is unlikely to be the sole driver of systemic burdens. Managing proximity to development and waste infrastructure may reduce wildlife microplastic exposure.
cards.why_you: Loosely relevant: a neuroscientist may find the systemic, non-local exposure pattern an interesting parallel to how environmental factors reach the brain.

cards.title: Scale-rich network-based metamaterials.
cards.post: Aim: To embed network heterogeneity into mechanical metamaterials and test whether multiscale variability yields properties unavailable to single-scale designs. Methods: Two-parameter scale-rich network models translated into physical materials, evaluated through simulations and experiments on elastic, nonlinear, dynamic and wave-control behaviour. Results: Scale-rich metamaterials showed highly tunable elastic anisotropy, delocalised nonlinear deformation with high energy absorption, enhanced energy dissipation under dynamic loading and programmable elastic-wave control. Conclusion: The framework provides a minimal, universal model for engineering multifunctional materials whose mechanics emerge from scale diversity, and opens new questions for network science.
cards.why_you: Loosely relevant: the idea that function arises from multiscale connectivity echoes your interest in brain networks and neurodynamics.

cards.title: Psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression: fMRI-measured brain mechanisms
cards.post: Aim: To characterise the brain mechanisms, measured with fMRI, of psilocybin-assisted treatment for treatment-resistant depression. Methods: Pre and post-treatment fMRI measuring cerebral blood flow and BOLD resting-state connectivity in 19 patients treated with psilocybin and psychological support, with 16 having quality scans. Results: All 19 patients showed reduced depressive symptoms at one week, and 47% responded at five weeks. Reduced amygdala blood flow correlated with symptom reduction, and default-mode connectivity increased post-treatment. Conclusion: Post-treatment brain changes differ from acute psychedelic effects yet relate to clinical outcomes. The authors propose a reset mechanism, with small sample size as a limitation.
cards.why_you: Directly relevant to your psilocybin for depression work and to the default-mode and amygdala mechanisms you study.

cards.title: Psilocybin desynchronizes the human brain
cards.post: Aim: To determine how psilocybin reshapes large-scale human brain functional connectivity and whether these changes relate to the subjective experience and lasting effects. Methods: Longitudinal precision fMRI with roughly 18 scans per participant in healthy adults, before, during and for three weeks after 25 mg psilocybin or 40 mg methylphenidate, with a further psilocybin dose 6-12 months later. Results: Psilocybin produced over threefold greater acute connectivity change than methylphenidate, driven by cross-scale desynchronisation, strongest in the default mode network. Anterior hippocampus to default mode connectivity stayed reduced for weeks. Conclusion: Persistent hippocampal-default mode reduction may be a neuroanatomical correlate of the proplasticity and therapeutic effects of psychedelics. The sample is small and healthy-volunteer based.
cards.why_you: Core to your interest in psychedelics as neuroplastogens and to the default-mode and hippocampal network changes you measure.

cards.title: qsiprep 26.2.0 released
cards.post: qsiprep 26.2.0 is a release of the diffusion MRI preprocessing pipeline, with a new output-spaces option, per-output resolutions, improved QC summaries and bug fixes. It suits researchers running diffusion preprocessing.
cards.why_you: Useful if you process diffusion data alongside your PET and EEG pipelines; no direct link to current projects.

cards.title: tvb-root 3.0.0a1 released
cards.post: tvb-root 3.0.0a1 is an early alpha of a multi-model simulation framework with a pure Python backend, Numba code generation and parameter sweeps, plus tutorial notebooks. APIs may still change.
cards.why_you: Relevant to your whole-brain and neural mass modelling interests, though the release is early and unstable.

cards.title: nibabel 5.5.0 released
cards.post: nibabel 5.5.0 is a feature release of the Python neuroimaging I/O library, adding DICOM mixed-orientation filtering, complex image support in get_fdata and reorientation improvements. It requires Python 3.11 or later.
cards.why_you: Relevant to your imaging analysis code if you read and reorient NIfTI or CIFTI files in Python.

cards.title: EEG-DL: A deep learning library for EEG signal classification, with 26 network architectures.
cards.post: EEG-DL is a new TensorFlow library offering 26 deep learning architectures for EEG signal classification, with tutorials and a demo. It is a recent repository with modest community uptake.
cards.why_you: Relevant if you explore deep learning classifiers for EEG, though its maturity is uncertain for research use.
